result: The authors identify PIGS as a novel scene-selective region in the posterior intraparietal gyrus that is consistently detectable across subjects (n=59), populations, sessions, and scanners (3T and 7T). PIGS was found in all tested individuals and showed reproducibility across different experimental conditions.
evaluation: All three reviewers affirm the identification and reproducibility of PIGS. Reviewer 3 states the authors 'firmly establish the location and selectivity of the new area through a series of well-crafted controlled experiments' and notes they 'show that it appears in much the same location in different subjects, with different magnetic field strengths, and with different stimulus sets.' The editor confirms 'evidence for these important findings is solid.'

result: PIGS is anatomically distinct from other scene-selective areas and adjacent regions. It is located within the posterior intraparietal gyrus outside the POS, adjacent to IPS3-4, and separate from V6 (which is within the POS), TOS/OPA (which overlaps with V3A/B and IPS0), and other scene-selective areas based on anatomical landmarks and retinotopic mapping.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the anatomical characterization. The editor notes the authors 'delineate the anatomical location of PIGS and functionally differentiate it from nearby V6 and OPA.' Reviewer 3 confirms the authors 'firmly establish the location and selectivity of the new area' with 'strong' evidence. No concerns are raised about the anatomical localization data.

result: PIGS shows selective sensitivity to ego-motion in scenes, responding significantly more strongly to coherently changing scenes (implying ego-motion) compared to incoherently changing scenes. This sensitivity distinguishes PIGS from other scene-selective areas (RSC/MPA, TOS/OPA, PPA/TPA), which did not show significant modulation to ego-motion.
evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the ego-motion findings, they express reservations about the strength of the conclusion. Reviewer 2 states 'the results show that this scene-selective region is sensitive to visual cues that reflect ego-motion but not that it is "key" to encoding ego-motion' and notes 'there are many differences between the two types of stimuli used to test ego-motion and greater characterization of this scene-selective region will be needed to confirm this conclusion.' The editor similarly notes 'further investigations as to the role of this region in processing ego-motion will be needed to confirm this conclusion.'

result: PIGS shows significant scene-selective activity across multiple experiments and stimulus sets, with activity levels comparable to other scene-selective areas and significantly higher than adjacent area V6.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the scene-selectivity findings. Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'firmly establish the location and selectivity of the new area' and that 'the evidence presented is strong.' The functional differentiation from V6 is explicitly mentioned by the editor as being solidly demonstrated.

result: PIGS does not respond selectively to simple motion stimuli (radially moving concentric rings), distinguishing it from TOS/OPA which shows strong motion selectivity. This differential response pattern suggests PIGS is involved in encoding higher-level ego-motion cues rather than simple motion.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes the authors 'further clarify that the area is not generically motion selective by showing that it does not respond to biological motion without an egomotion component to it.' This functional dissociation is accepted without challenge by reviewers.

result: PIGS does not respond selectively to biological motion, showing no significant difference between biological versus translational motion conditions. This indicates PIGS does not respond to all types of complex motion.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 affirms this finding, stating the authors 'show that it does not respond to biological motion without an egomotion component to it.' This is presented as evidence that PIGS is not generically motion-selective.

result: Previous studies may have missed smaller scene-selective areas like PIGS due to methodological limitations including excessive spatial smoothing, focus on larger sites, and technical constraints of early fMRI. At the single-subject level with low smoothing, multiple smaller scene-selective sites are detectable.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly affirms this explanation, noting the authors 'show that the area can be missed with too much smoothing, thus providing a case for why it has not been previously described.' This methodological insight is accepted by reviewers as explaining why PIGS was not previously identified.

result: While V6 also shows some response to coherently changing scenes, the level of ego-motion selectivity is significantly weaker in V6 compared to PIGS. The authors conclude PIGS contributes to scene encoding and ego-motion within scenes, while V6 is involved in detecting optic flow caused by ego-motion.
evaluation: The functional differentiation between PIGS and V6 is explicitly affirmed by the editor who notes the authors 'functionally differentiate it from nearby V6.' No reviewer challenges the comparative data between PIGS and V6.

result: PIGS responds selectively to a wide variety of scene types across five different stimulus sets (indoor/outdoor, natural/manmade), with response levels comparable to other scene-selective areas. The scene-selective response is not limited to a single subset of scenes.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes the authors tested PIGS 'with different stimulus sets' as part of establishing its selectivity. The variety of stimuli is implicitly accepted as demonstrating broad scene-selectivity.
